### Observed differences

- All six qualifying items concern resource allocation on six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22); no control-flow or timing items passed the thresholds. [screening]
- In the earlier window, one recurring group of about eight resources dominated all six activities: User_37 held the largest single share on every one of them (about 8–11 in 100 assignments), and together with its recurring companions the group accounted for roughly 48–56 in 100 of each activity's assignments. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- In the later window, that group's combined share fell to roughly 3–18 in 100 (about 3–11 on five of the six activities), with User_37 dropping to about 0–5 in 100 and disappearing from the top shares on A13, A14 and A17. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- A largely different group took over the work: led by User_3, which went from essentially 0 to about 8–9 in 100 on every activity, and including User_42, which rose on all six activities (for example from about 5 to about 9 in 100 on A01 and from about 5 to about 12 in 100 on A22), this group's combined share grew from about 4–9 in 100 to about 41–52 in 100. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- The pooled remainder of many minor resources kept a roughly stable share (about 38–48 in 100 before, 38–45 in 100 after), so the shift is an exchange between named resource groups rather than a move to or from the long tail. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- The six differences are of similar size (cosine dissimilarity about 0.42–0.45) and each is larger than about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits; the profiles rest on roughly 130–260 observations per window (lowest about 131–137 for A22), so none rests on a handful of cases. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- Screening context: the resource family produced 6 items where about 0.004 would be expected if nothing had changed, while the control-flow family (37 units) and the time family (36 units) produced none (0.18 and 0.018 expected); A13 and A14 have identical profiles, so the six items describe at most five distinct activity profiles. [screening, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility of a change in resource allocation: in the later window, the work on activities A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was handled by a largely different set of resources than in the earlier window, with a group of about eight holders (largest: User_37) falling from roughly half of each activity's assignments to a few in 100, and a new group led by User_3 and User_42 rising from almost none to roughly 40–50 in 100. The hypothesis is direct (the items are the allocation profiles themselves), consistent in direction across all six activities, and the resource family's 6 items are orders of magnitude above the roughly 0.004 expected without a change, so the pattern as a whole is not what an unchanged process typically produces. Limitations: A13 and A14 share one identical profile, so the items are not fully independent; and because the codes are anonymous, the evidence cannot distinguish a reallocation of work among continuing resources from a change in the resource pool itself, with earlier codes dropping out and new codes appearing — the profiles alone cannot separate these two readings. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, screening]

Other differences: none qualified at the configured thresholds — the control-flow family (37 units tested) and the time family (36 units tested) produced no items. [screening]
